text:
This design review covers the proposed battery backup arrangement for the trackside signal cabinets on the Eastmere branch line, a fictional route serving four rural stations. The review was requested by the Signalling Power Group after a series of short outages at the Millbrook crossing in the spring, although those outages were later traced to a faulty contactor rather than to the supply design itself. The group's lead engineer, Renata Oyelaran, asked that the review focus on whether a lithium iron phosphate pack could replace the existing lead acid strings without changing the cabinet footprint. Background material, including the procurement history and the vendor shortlist, is held in the group's document store and is not reproduced here.

The existing cabinets were installed in the late nineteen nineties and have been refurbished twice since. The original specification called for a lead acid string sized for four hours of standby, but a later revision reduced this to ninety minutes after the signal upgrade at the junction. Records of that revision are incomplete, and the group has not been able to confirm who approved the change, so this review treats the ninety minute figure as a working requirement rather than a verified one.

The evaluation rests on a bench test of two prototype cabinets run over eleven weeks at the Harrowgate Junction depot. Each prototype was loaded with a simulated signal demand profile drawn from logged operating data, and the packs were cycled through forty discharge events of varying depth. Because only two cabinets were built, the results describe a narrow slice of conditions and cannot be read as a population estimate.

Responsibility for the trial was split between three groups. The Depot Test Bay team owned the rig and the daily checks, the Asset Analysis team owned the fault data, and the Signalling Power Group owned the design and the final recommendation. Coordination meetings were held on Tuesdays, and the minutes record that the handover of the logger calibration sheet took longer than planned.

The logging software used in the test bay was written in-house by the Tooling Office and exports data in a comma separated format. The logger clock drifted by roughly four seconds per day for part of the trial, which was corrected in post-processing. A small number of rows were also dropped during an October export because of a buffer setting, and these were recovered from a backup copy. The recovery was checked by comparing totals, but no row-level comparison was carried out.

The main observation is that the lithium pack held the cabinet signal load for the required ninety minutes in all forty discharge events, while the lead acid reference string fell short of that duration in nine of them. Early results suggest the lithium arrangement may reduce the number of unplanned site visits, although this is an inference from a short test and has not been confirmed in the field.

The estimate of charge retention carries wide uncertainty. Across the forty events the measured capacity varied by about eleven percent between the two prototypes, and the confidence interval on end of discharge voltage spans roughly 0.3 volts. Neither figure is large enough to rule out a meaningful difference from the reference string at the lower temperatures seen in January, which the bench could not reproduce because the test bay heater was out of service for three weeks.

It should be stressed that the forty discharge events were not randomised across the test period. Eighteen were run during the summer months when ambient temperature was higher, and the remaining twenty-two were run in autumn. The comparison between those seasons was not planned in advance and is included here only to show that the result does not depend entirely on one season.

A separate desk study by the Asset Analysis team, based on fault records from four other branch lines, found a lower failure rate for lead acid cabinets than the bench results would predict. The desk study used maintenance logs that record faults by visit rather than by cabinet, so the two sources are not directly comparable, and the team noted that its authors had not seen the bench data before drafting.

The prototype cabinets were transported to the depot on a hired flatbed in July and were reinstalled on bench stands within two days. Two cooling fans were replaced during the trial under the standard warranty, and the replacement dates have been noted in the maintenance log for completeness.

The design assumes that the charger output on the existing feeder stays within the window the lithium management system expects. That window was taken from a datasheet for a comparable pack, and nobody on the review panel has verified it against the actual feeder voltage at the four stations, which was measured only once in August by the field survey team.

Before the group adopts the lithium arrangement, three conditions should be met. The feeder voltage must be logged continuously for at least one full quarter at every station, the cabinet thermal behaviour must be measured through a winter period in the test bay, and the fault data must be re-coded by cabinet so that it can be compared directly with the bench results. If any of these conditions is not met, the recommendation should be treated as provisional and the existing lead acid strings should remain in service.

Overall the review judges the lithium option promising but not yet established. The panel recommends a second test campaign before any procurement decision, and it notes that the final figures may move once the field logs are complete.

This report describes a two-winter field study conducted by the Tallow Ridge Energy Group, a small applied research team based in the town of Merrow Fell in the province of Ardane. The team's three engineers and one data analyst worked alongside a regional installer, Brightwater Fitting Co., which handled hardware swaps, and a cooperative utility, the Halden Power Cooperative, which supplied interval meter data under a research agreement signed in early 2024. Most of the logistics were routine. Installers scheduled visits in batches of forty, and the team used an internal dashboard called Lumen Ledger to track data gaps, which turned out to be the most time-consuming part of the project.

The question was narrow. Households that already had rooftop solar panels were offered a home battery, and the team wanted to know how much the battery reduced electricity drawn from the grid during the evening, when demand peaks and the cooperative's time-of-use tariff charges the most. Enrolment ran from March to August 2024. In total 4,312 households received a 9.6 kilowatt-hour lithium battery, and 4,198 households with solar panels but no battery served as a comparison group. All homes had systems between 3 and 7 kilowatts, and all had 15-minute interval meters.

The main result is clear. Across the first winter, battery-equipped households reduced their grid imports between 17:00 and 22:00 by 41 percent relative to matched comparison households, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 39 to 43 percent. The estimate came from a difference-in-differences model that compared each household with its own pre-installation baseline and with the change seen in the comparison group, and standard errors were clustered by postcode. A second winter, in a separate district with 1,106 households, produced a reduction of 38 percent. The two estimates differ by a few points, which the team regards as ordinary variation between districts rather than a sign that the effect is unstable.

The comparison is not a randomised trial, and that matters. Households chose to take a battery when offered, and those who chose it may have had higher evening usage or greater interest in energy management before the study began. Matching on fourteen household covariates reduced the imbalance between groups, bringing the standardised mean difference on baseline evening use from 0.31 to 0.06, but matching cannot adjust for motivations that the meters do not record.

The second district was chosen partly for convenience. Its installer was already working with the team, and its households had slightly newer inverters. That second point turns out to matter, as discussed below. Installation dates were staggered so that the last batch of households in each district had about two months of pre-installation data, and the team checked whether the seasonal pattern in the comparison group tracked the treated group before installation. It did, within the noise of the data.

The results also depend on the tariff. Halden's evening peak window runs from 17:00 to 21:00 at a rate of 0.31 units of currency per kilowatt-hour, with a flat off-peak rate. Savings from shifting load are largest where the peak price is high relative to the off-peak price, and the study did not test a flat tariff, a steeper tariff, or a region with different peak timing. Readers should not assume that a 41 percent reduction in grid imports carries over to a market where the evening rate is close to the daytime rate.

Summer results are weaker in evidence. A one-month summer sub-study covered 212 households, and its point estimate was a reduction of about 12 percent, but the interval was wide, running from roughly 2 to 22 percent. The team did not report a summer finding as established and treats the figure as a hypothesis for future work. The winter result should be read as a winter result.

Lifetime economics rest on an assumption the study could not test. The battery cycle-degradation curve used in the team's cost model was taken from the manufacturer's specification, which projects about 2.1 percent capacity loss per year. The longest field record is eighteen months old, so ten-year behaviour is extrapolated, and a battery that degraded faster would reduce the evening savings that the winter results imply.

A separate and smaller pilot from 2023 points in a different direction. That study, run by another group with 88 households at a utility in the neighbouring region, found an evening import reduction of only 19 percent. The earlier households had inverters capped at discharge rates below 2 kilowatts, and the team's own sub-analysis suggests that discharge rate explains much of the gap. The explanation is plausible but not proven, because the older study did not record inverter model at the household level.

Before a utility or installer acts on these results, three conditions should be met. First, the inverters in the target homes should be able to discharge at no less than 3 kilowatts, since the team's dose-response check found that the reduction levelled off below that value. Second, the tariff should have a meaningful evening peak premium. Third, the purchaser should confirm the battery warranty terms against the degradation assumption above. Cost-effectiveness was not assessed, because the study measured grid imports rather than bills, and a reduction in imports is not the same as a reduction in what a household pays.

The team plans a third winter with a flat-tariff arm, funded through a provincial energy research grant with a decision expected in the first quarter of 2027. Data cleaning for the current report took about five months, mostly to reconcile meter timestamps across two firmware versions. The project lead handled the design and the grant reporting, one engineer managed the installer relationship, and the analyst maintained the cleaning pipeline. The raw data are held by the cooperative under its research agreement and are not publicly released.

The Ferndale Coast Analytics group maintains the nightly sales forecasting feed that supplies weekly volume estimates to replenishment planners for 118 stores in the fictional Saltmere region. The feed was rebuilt in March after a migration from an older batch scheduler called Tidewell to a streaming ingestion service known internally as Breakwater. The migration was delayed twice, once by a certificate renewal and once by a dispute over how promotional codes should be represented in the schema. Most of the audit work was carried out by three analysts, one of whom also owns the regional dashboard, so several checks were run in evenings and on weekends. The feed's output is consumed by planners who place orders on a weekly cycle, so a shift of even a few percent can change order quantities for slow-moving lines.

The audit asked a narrow question: whether the feed's weekly totals reflect what was actually sold, and if the totals do not match, where the difference begins. Two comparison sources were available. The first is the store ledger, a nightly export from each store's point-of-sale terminals that the finance operations group reconciles once a month. The second is the regional rollup, a dashboard aggregate built from the same terminals but routed through a separate transport path with its own buffering rules. Because the two sources are built differently, they can disagree for reasons unrelated to the feed, and the team treated any disagreement as something to explain rather than as a verdict.

The audit drew a stratified sample of 52 stores from the 118 in the region, selected to cover the three size tiers in proportion to their share of weekly volume. Nine weeks of raw terminal events for these stores were replayed through a staging copy of the feed, and the replayed totals were compared with both comparison sources. The replay was the only step that could isolate the feed from the other systems, which is why it carries most of the weight in this report.

Terminal events carry a local time offset, and Breakwater converts each event to a universal timestamp before applying a closing-time rule. The rule is defined in a configuration file maintained by the operations group, and it assigns any event stamped after 22:00 local time to the following business day. This rule was written for stores that close at 21:00, and a number of stores in the sample stay open later on weekends. The rule itself is documented, but the team found that its interaction with terminal clock offsets had never been tested as a combined case.

Validation proceeded in three passes. The first pass checked row counts between raw events and feed records, and it found no dropped rows, which ruled out a simple ingestion loss. The second pass compared daily totals against the ledger for a single store with known problems, and it confirmed that the discrepancy appeared on the same days as late-evening events. The third pass repeated the comparison for a different store with no clock issues, and the discrepancy disappeared. Each pass was small, and together they point toward the timestamp rule, though none of them tests the rule directly.

The principal finding is that transactions stamped after a store's local closing time are assigned to the following business day by the feed. In the sample, this moves about 1.8 percent of weekly volume from one week into the next, and the effect is concentrated in stores where the terminal clock was set to a different time zone during the March migration. Replay reproduced the shift in 38 of the 52 stores, which is the strongest single piece of evidence in the audit.

The ledger comparison supports this picture only partly. Weekly totals in the feed agree with the ledger within 0.3 percent for 41 of the 52 stores, and the remaining eleven show differences that reverse sign from one week to the next, which is what a timing shift would produce. The regional rollup tells a different story. In the western cluster of 14 stores, the rollup shows a persistent undercount of roughly 2.6 percent that does not reverse across the sample window, and that pattern is not visible in the ledger. The team suspects the rollup buffering, which can hold events for up to 40 minutes, but it has not confirmed this.

Taking the ledger and rollup results together, the audit team could not decide whether the western undercount is a feed fault, a rollup fault, or a real difference in how late-evening sales are buffered. The estimate of the persistent gap carries a 95 percent interval of plus or minus 1.1 percent. That interval is wide enough that a second data source would be needed before the figure is used in any planning decision.

The sample covers nine weeks, which is short for a feed that serves a full fiscal year. Seasonal promotions fell outside the window, and the audit did not examine the forecasting model that consumes the feed, so the report makes no claim about forecast accuracy. The ledger is also reconciled only monthly, which means the nine-week comparison relied on unreconciled figures for its final two weeks.

The analysis assumes that all terminals in a store share a single clock source. The team checked this for only six stores, by comparing terminal logs against a network time service, and it is possible that the other stores differ in ways the sample did not reveal.

Before the feed is changed, the team recommends that the timestamp rule be verified against two full fiscal months of ledger data, and that the western cluster be re-examined with the rollup transport path disabled. Until both checks are complete, planners should treat the weekly figures as accurate only to within about three percent.

Several other details did not change the conclusions. Log access went through a change board that meets on alternate Thursdays, which added about a week to the timeline. The regional dashboard is maintained by a separate group, and its owners were helpful but busy with a quarterly reporting cycle. Earlier audit notes from the migration period were found in a shared folder and were not used, because they described an earlier version of the feed. Those notes were written in the same style as the earlier change log, which made them easy to confuse with current records. The staging copy was refreshed twice during the audit, and both refreshes were logged in the team's change record.

items.meaning: A summary must keep that the feed's closing-time rule shifts about 1.8 percent of weekly volume between adjacent weeks in the sample.

items.quotation: The sample covers nine weeks, which is short for a feed that serves a full fiscal year.
items.meaning: A summary must keep that the nine-week sample is too short to represent a full fiscal year.

items.quotation: The analysis assumes that all terminals in a store share a single clock source.
items.meaning: A summary must keep that the analysis assumes a single clock source per store, which was checked in only six stores.

items.quotation: The regional rollup tells a different story.
items.meaning: A summary must keep that the regional rollup shows a persistent undercount that the ledger does not confirm, so the two sources conflict.

items.quotation: The estimate of the persistent gap carries a 95 percent interval of plus or minus 1.1 percent.
items.meaning: A summary must keep that the western undercount estimate is wide, with a 95 percent interval of plus or minus 1.1 percent.

items.quotation: Until both checks are complete, planners should treat the weekly figures as accurate only to within about three percent.
items.meaning: A summary must keep that planners should not rely on the weekly figures beyond about three percent accuracy until two specified checks are complete.

text:
The bench study described here was commissioned by the clinical engineering office of the Marrowdale regional hospital network, which wanted to know whether the occlusion alarm on its general-purpose volumetric infusion pumps responded quickly enough when a downstream line became blocked. The work was carried out by the Ostrander Field Group, a five-person team that normally handles equipment acceptance testing for the network. The lead engineer coordinated the protocol, two technicians ran the rigs on alternating shifts, and a biostatistician from the network's quality office reviewed the analysis plan before any data were collected. The study was planned over several months, and the protocol was fixed before the first trial was run, which the committee later checked against the dated protocol file. No device manufacturer funded the study, and the team had no contract with any vendor during the period.

The test rig consisted of a gravity-fed saline reservoir, a carriage that held each pump at a fixed mounting height, a length of standard administration tubing, and a pneumatic clamp mounted about forty centimetres downstream of the pump outlet. The clamp could be closed at three controlled rates, labelled slow, moderate and abrupt, so that the resulting pressure rise imitated different kinds of blockage. A pressure transducer logged line pressure at 50 samples per second, and a separate timer recorded the interval between clamp closure and the first audible and visual alarm. Each trial began with the pump running at a set rate for two minutes so that the line reached a steady state before closure. The clamp was cleaned and checked for leaks at the start of each session, and any trial with a visible leak at the connector was discarded and repeated.

The team tested 14 pump units drawn from three hardware revisions, labelled A, B and C in the report. Revision C carried a revised pressure filter and a shortened detection window in its firmware. Revision C units accounted for all 2,160 trials in the main analysis, with 720 trials in each of three test campaigns run in different calendar months. Each campaign covered five flow rates, three tubing sets and the three closure rates. Revisions A and B were run only in the first campaign as comparison arms, with 360 trials each. The rig was recalibrated against a reference gauge before every session, and the revision label on each unit was covered until the data were locked, so operators did not know which revision they were testing.

The principal finding is that revision C raised its alarm within the 20-second limit set by the network's acceptance standard in 2,094 of the 2,160 trials, a rate of 96.9 percent. In the first campaign, revision A and revision B met the same limit in 88.4 and 91.2 percent of their comparison trials. The advantage of revision C was largest at the abrupt closure rate and the highest flow setting, where median alarm latency fell from about 17 seconds to about 9 seconds. Those medians were calculated only from trials in which an alarm sounded.

The second finding is that the result replicated across the three campaigns, which were run in different months by the same team. Revision C met the 20-second limit in 697 of 720 trials in the first campaign, 701 of 720 in the second and 696 of 720 in the third, giving campaign rates of 96.8, 97.4 and 96.7 percent. The campaign-level spread was small, and no single campaign drove the overall result.

Uncertainty around the overall estimate is still worth stating. Treating the trials as independent, the 95 percent interval for the within-limit rate was 96.2 to 97.7 percent. Trials on the same unit were not fully independent, however, so the true interval is probably somewhat wider than this calculation suggests.

The team also reviewed incident reports from the network's wards. Between the release of revision C and the end of the study, one ward logged two occlusions in which the alarm sounded more than 30 seconds after a nurse noticed that flow had stopped. The team could not reproduce delays of that size on the rig, and the reports did not record the tubing set or flow rate, so the team could not determine whether the bench conditions matched the ward conditions. These reports were treated as unresolved rather than explained away.

All trials used room-temperature normal saline. The team did not test blood, lipid emulsions or other viscous fluids, and the findings say nothing about how the alarm behaves when the fluid thickens or the line carries air. Limits of this kind matter because the network's wards use the pumps for a wide range of infusions, not only the simple fluids used on the bench.

The closure rates were chosen to approximate blockage dynamics the team believed were typical, drawn from published test notes and a discussion with the network's anesthesia staff. The team recorded that choice in the protocol before any data were collected. The team did not measure real blockage pressure curves on patients, so the assumption that the three closure rates bracket clinical conditions remains untested.

The interval describes one rig model at one site and does not capture variation between rigs, which was not estimated because only one rig was built. A second rig would have cost the team about three weeks of setup time, and the committee judged that delay acceptable only for the final decision, not for the bench study.

The team recommends that the network not rely on these results for high-viscosity infusions until a separate campaign using viscous fluids has been completed. Before any clinical rollout, the revision C firmware should be run on at least two independent rigs and the ward incident reports should be re-reviewed with flow rate and tubing set recorded.

The report was reviewed internally by the quality office and sent to the network's pump committee in late summer. The committee asked for the raw transducer logs, which the team provided as a sealed archive. Its reviewers also asked for a short plain-language summary for the ward managers, which the team wrote in two pages and which is not reproduced here. The rig was moved to a storage room after the final campaign and has since been recalibrated, a logistical step that does not affect the results.

items.quotation: The second finding is that the result replicated across the three campaigns, which were run in different months by the same team.
items.meaning: The 96.9 percent result held in all three separate campaigns, with campaign rates between 96.7 and 97.4 percent, so a summary must say it replicated.

items.quotation: the 95 percent interval for the within-limit rate was 96.2 to 97.7 percent
items.meaning: The confidence interval is 96.2 to 97.7 percent, and it is probably slightly too narrow because trials on the same unit were not fully independent.

items.meaning: The results apply only to room-temperature saline, so a summary must not extend them to blood, lipid emulsions or viscous fluids.

text:
This report documents the acceptance test for a leading-edge erosion coating applied to twelve blade sets supplied to the Ferrow Ridge wind park. The test was commissioned by the procurement office of the operator, Lanterne Energy Group, and carried out by an invented test team at the Ostmere Materials Laboratory between March and May 2026. The coating under evaluation is a two-layer polyurethane system with a ceramic filler, listed in the purchase order as Coating Grade B. The acceptance criteria were agreed in advance between the operator and the supplier, Halvane Surface Works, and set a pass line of no more mass loss than the incumbent product under identical conditions. The supplier prepared all coupons in its own facility before shipment.

The operator had accepted blades with a single-layer system, Coating Grade A, in earlier contracts. Inspections at two older sites, however, showed pitting near the blade tips after about three seasons of service. The procurement office therefore asked for a bench comparison of the new system against the incumbent under a rain-erosion rig. The rig uses a rotating arm carrying test coupons, fed by a water spray at a fixed droplet size set by the nozzle specification. Marisol Quenby led the rig work as test engineer, Dov Ansary handled surface analysis, and Harrow Pell acted as the procurement liaison. Shipping of coupons in padded crates, rotation of the arm counterweights and the full calibration log are recorded in the appendix and are not needed to follow the results.

Twelve coupons of each coating were exposed to simulated rain at a tip speed of 90 metres per second, giving 400 hours of equivalent exposure in total. Coupons were cut from flat panels of the same laminate used on the blade shells, cleaned with a solvent wipe and cured under the supplier's schedule before testing. The arm was run in blocks of ten hours with cooling pauses between blocks so that the water temperature stayed within a narrow band. Each coupon was weighed and its surface profile measured with a stylus profilometer every 50 hours. Each system came from a single coating batch, so the comparison rests on one production run per product and on twelve coupons per arm of the test.

At 400 hours the incumbent coupons had lost a mean of 41 milligrams each, while the two-layer coupons had lost a mean of 19 milligrams each. Early results suggest that the two-layer system may reduce rain-erosion mass loss by roughly half relative to the incumbent under these bench conditions. Both systems were below the agreed pass line on the mass loss criterion, which the analysts noted was a lenient standard. The gap between the two systems was small during the first 150 hours and widened after that point. The analysts tentatively attributed the widening to a settling of the filler in the outer layer of the new coating, but they did not measure the filler distribution directly.

The comparison is based on only twelve coupons per coating, and the coupon-to-coupon scatter was large. Using a simple two-sample comparison, the 95 percent interval on that difference runs from about 9 to 35 milligrams, so the true reduction could be considerably smaller than half. The analysts did not run a second batch and did not test whether the result holds at other tip speeds. A single bench run cannot separate a real improvement from a favourable draw of coupons.

Surface roughness told a similar but weaker story. Mean roughness of the two-layer coupons rose by 0.3 micrometres over the test, against 1.1 micrometres for the incumbent. Surface roughness of the two-layer system grew more slowly than the incumbent, which may matter for aerodynamic efficiency. The link between roughness at this scale and power loss has not been measured on these blades, so the roughness result should be read as a sign of surface durability rather than as a measure of energy output.

The rig does not reproduce hail, ultraviolet ageing or thermal cycling, and none of those were included in this acceptance test. The results therefore apply to rain erosion alone, and a pass on this test should not be read as a general endorsement of the coating for the operator's climate range. The droplet size chosen for the rig matches the nozzle specification used in an earlier coastal study, and that assumption has not been checked against the inland sites where two of the new turbines will stand. Inland rain is often lighter and may carry smaller drops, which could change the ranking of the two systems.

Field exposure of the new coating so far covers only six months, which is too short to compare with the three-season history of the incumbent. The field data from the older sites therefore remain the strongest evidence of long-term behaviour, and they describe a different product. The field team has agreed to inspect the first installed blades at the three-month and six-month marks, but no pitting measurements are yet available for the new coating.

Before the operator relies on these results for the wider order, the field trial must run for at least two full seasons on at least one site, and the inland droplet assumption must be checked with a short rig run. The analysts recommend that the procurement office treat the bench result as a reason to continue the trial, not as proof of improvement. A repeat rig test with a second coating batch and a range of droplet sizes would narrow the uncertainty considerably and is proposed as the next step in the programme.

items.quotation: Early results suggest that the two-layer system may reduce rain-erosion mass loss by roughly half relative to the incumbent under these bench conditions.
items.meaning: A summary must keep that the two-layer coating may roughly halve rain-erosion mass loss compared with the incumbent, under bench conditions only.

items.quotation: Surface roughness of the two-layer system grew more slowly than the incumbent, which may matter for aerodynamic efficiency
items.meaning: A summary must keep that the two-layer coating's surface roughness grew more slowly than the incumbent's, a tentative sign of durability whose link to power loss is unmeasured.

items.quotation: the 95 percent interval on that difference runs from about 9 to 35 milligrams
items.meaning: A summary must keep that with only twelve coupons per coating the uncertainty is wide, so the true reduction could be much smaller than half.

items.quotation: The rig does not reproduce hail, ultraviolet ageing or thermal cycling
items.meaning: A summary must keep that the results cover rain erosion only and do not show suitability for other weather or ageing conditions.

items.meaning: A summary must keep that the droplet size assumption, based on a coastal study, is untested for the inland sites where the turbines will stand.

items.quotation: Field exposure of the new coating so far covers only six months
items.meaning: A summary must keep that the field evidence for the new coating is too short to compare with the incumbent's three-season record.

items.quotation: Before the operator relies on these results for the wider order, the field trial must run for at least two full seasons on at least one site
items.meaning: A summary must keep that the field trial must run for at least two full seasons before the results are relied on for the wider order.

text:
The Lantern Ridge fraud analytics group prepared this report to describe an early evaluation of a gradient-boosted classifier for flagging card-not-present transactions. The model was trained on eighteen months of anonymized transaction records supplied by a regional card processor under a data-sharing agreement that the group's legal office renewed in the spring. Most of the engineering work was carried out by a small team of four analysts and one platform engineer, and the team's work was tracked on a shared board that is not reproduced here. Readers who need operational details should consult the internal change log, which records each retraining run and its configuration.

The training code was written in Python and orchestrated with a workflow scheduler maintained by the platform group. Feature tables were stored in a columnar warehouse, and each analysis lived in a notebook that was reviewed by a second analyst before results were shared. That review practice was adopted after an earlier study was found to contain a join error that inflated apparent recall. Nobody on the current team worked on that earlier study, and its details are kept in the group's retrospective archive.

The evaluation used a holdout window of six weeks drawn from the most recent period available at the time of the study. That window contained roughly 212,000 transactions, of which about 1,430 were labelled as confirmed fraud after chargeback review. The small number of positive cases is the main reason the results below should be read cautiously. Because chargebacks can take up to ninety days to resolve, the most recent part of the holdout may contain transactions that were still unresolved when the labels were pulled, which means some true fraud was probably recorded as legitimate.

The first principal finding concerns precision at a fixed alert volume, which is the metric the fraud operations group uses to size its review queue. On the holdout window, the classifier achieved a precision of 0.41 at the operating threshold selected during development, compared with 0.27 for the rules engine currently in production. Early results suggest that this gain holds across the three merchant categories tested, although the sample within each category was small.

The second principal finding concerns reviewer workload. The model reduced the number of alerts that were ultimately cleared by manual review by about 18 percent at the same recall level, which may translate into lower reviewer workload if the result survives a longer test. This second finding rests on the same six-week window and should be treated as a secondary observation rather than an independent confirmation.

The confidence interval around the precision figure is wide. With roughly 1,430 positive labels and a precision estimate near 0.41, a bootstrap interval spans from about 0.35 to 0.47, so the true advantage over the rules engine could be considerably smaller than the point estimate suggests.

The group first tried a logistic baseline in the previous spring, but it was abandoned after the feature pipeline proved fragile when the processor changed its merchant code format. The gradient-boosted model replaced it after a second round of feature engineering. Some of the features the model relies on, such as velocity counts over rolling windows, depend on timestamp handling that was revised in the summer, and the team has not yet verified that the historical features were recomputed with the corrected logic.

The evaluation assumes that the labels in the holdout window are complete and unbiased. Transactions that were never disputed are treated as legitimate, which is only true if cardholders reliably notice and report fraud. Fraud that goes unreported would make the model look worse than it is, but cases where alerts prompted reviewers to contact cardholders and confirm a transaction may have produced labels that favour the model in ways the team cannot measure.

The operating threshold was chosen to match the alert volume the review team said it could handle, which in practice meant accepting a lower recall than the model could in principle reach. This tradeoff is a business decision rather than a statistical one. The group expects to revisit it once reviewers have worked with the new queue for a month.

The study was run on a shared cluster with a fixed compute budget, and the team limited the hyperparameter search to 40 configurations. The search was not nested inside the cross-validation folds, so the operating threshold may be slightly optimistic. The group plans to rerun threshold selection on a separate validation window before any change to production is proposed.

The results cover card-not-present transactions only. Card-present transactions, which make up a little under a third of volume in the source data, were excluded because the processor's device fingerprint fields are missing for most of those records. Nothing in this report should be read as evidence about that segment.

A separate offline replay run by the operations group, using a slightly different threshold, produced a precision of 0.33, which is closer to the rules engine than the headline figure. The two runs differ in how duplicate transactions were handled, and the team has not yet determined which handling matches production. Until that is resolved, the gap between the models could plausibly fall anywhere between those two values.

Before any change to the production alerting path, the group recommends that three conditions be met. The first is a replay on a fresh window of at least twelve weeks with labels aged at least ninety days. The second is a reconciliation of the duplicate-handling difference between the two runs. The third is sign-off from the fraud operations lead confirming that the review queue can absorb the change in alert mix. The group does not recommend acting on the present results alone.

The findings are best read as a promising first signal and a reason to design a longer study, not as a settled judgement about the classifier. The next report in this series will describe the replay results and whether the conditions above were met.

items.quotation: On the holdout window, the classifier achieved a precision of 0.41 at the operating threshold selected during development, compared with 0.27 for the rules engine currently in production.
items.meaning: A summary must keep that the classifier's precision was 0.41 versus 0.27 for the rules engine on the six-week holdout window, a tentative result.

items.quotation: The model reduced the number of alerts that were ultimately cleared by manual review by about 18 percent at the same recall level, which may translate into lower reviewer workload if the result survives a longer test.
items.meaning: A summary must keep that the model may cut manually cleared alerts by about 18 percent, a secondary and unconfirmed observation from the same window.

items.quotation: The confidence interval around the precision figure is wide.
items.meaning: A summary must keep that the precision gap has a wide interval, roughly 0.35 to 0.47, so the true advantage may be smaller.

items.quotation: The evaluation assumes that the labels in the holdout window are complete and unbiased.
items.meaning: A summary must keep that the results depend on untested assumptions about complete and unbiased fraud labels.

items.quotation: The results cover card-not-present transactions only.
items.meaning: A summary must keep that the findings do not extend to card-present transactions, which were excluded.

items.quotation: A separate offline replay run by the operations group, using a slightly different threshold, produced a precision of 0.33, which is closer to the rules engine than the headline figure.
items.meaning: A summary must keep that a conflicting replay produced precision of 0.33, so the true gap is uncertain.

items.quotation: The group does not recommend acting on the present results alone.
items.meaning: A summary must keep that the group advises against acting on these results until replay, reconciliation and operations sign-off conditions are met.

text:
This field-trial report describes a twelve-month evaluation of an adaptive dimming controller for municipal street lights in the invented town of Harrowmere Vale. The controller reduces lamp output between midnight and dawn based on pedestrian counts from roadside sensors, within limits set by a schedule approved by the local council. The trial was run by the Eastbrook Lighting Research Group, a small team of four engineers and one data analyst, under a grant from a regional energy office. Background on the council's older sodium lamps and the procurement history is kept in the appendix and is not repeated here.

The trial covered 146 lamp posts split across three districts. Two districts, Cinder Row and Millbank Lane, received the adaptive controller, while the third, Quarry Hill, kept fixed-schedule dimming as a comparison. Assignment was made by district rather than by lamp because the council's maintenance crews asked that each street be serviced as a unit. The team installed the controllers in March and collected data through the following February, logging readings every five minutes. Logistics such as the replacement of two faulty photocells in June and a dispute with a contractor over conduit access are recorded in the team logbook. They do not bear on the energy figures.

The primary outcome was metered energy use per lamp per night. Across the trial year, adaptive districts used 22 percent less energy per lamp than the fixed-schedule comparison district, with a 95 percent interval of 17 to 27 percent. This result came from the circuit meters and was the basis for the team's initial recommendation. The meters were read by the council's electrical contractor, whose staff also handled routine repairs, so the readings were collected alongside other site work.

The second source was a resident survey run by the council's community office in two waves, one in May and one in January. Respondents in the adaptive districts reported more frequent difficulty seeing kerbs and pavement edges at night, and the difference was largest among respondents over sixty-five. Incident records from the police liaison office, however, showed no increase in reported trips or falls in those districts over the same period. The survey returned 418 usable forms, a response rate of 31 percent, and the team could not confirm whether residents who felt less safe were more likely to return the form.

The disagreement between these sources is the central difficulty of the report. The energy data point clearly toward the adaptive controller, while the survey suggests a perceived cost in visibility that the incident data do not confirm. The team considered three explanations. The survey may have measured perception rather than actual hazard. The dimming curve in the adaptive controller may create abrupt step changes that residents notice even when visibility is adequate. Or the survey sample may have been drawn toward residents who already had concerns about the lights. None of these explanations could be tested within the trial period, and the team has not ranked them.

The metering also has limits. Meters were installed at the circuit level, and each circuit served between 22 and 31 lamps. The per-lamp figure therefore assumes equal load across lamps on a circuit, which may not hold where older and newer fittings were mixed. The team checked this assumption against a sample of 12 individually metered posts and found agreement within 4 percent. That sample was small, however, and the contractor chose the posts, so the check may not represent the whole network.

The controller was designed for a particular set of conditions, and the trial did not test all of them. The trial took place in a temperate coastal climate with mild winters. Results may not transfer to districts with heavy snowfall or long dark winters, where lamps run for more hours and the savings profile would differ. The pedestrian sensors were calibrated for movement at walking pace and were not tested against cyclists or vehicles stopping at the kerb. The team also assumed that residents' use of the streets would stay roughly constant through the year, and the trial period did not include a major local event or roadworks that might have changed the pattern.

A further untested assumption concerns light levels. The controller assumes that the council's minimum lighting standard is still met at reduced output. Lux measurements taken at 40 points showed compliance at 90 percent of points in the adaptive districts, against 97 percent in the comparison district. The team has not established whether the seven-point gap is a measurement artefact or a real shortfall. Until it is resolved, the compliance figure should be treated as uncertain rather than as evidence that the standard was met.

The team recommends that the council not adopt the adaptive controller across the whole town until two conditions are met. The first is a second trial season in a district with a different climate, long enough to cover a winter with heavy use. The second is a resident survey with a response rate high enough to test whether the visibility concern persists, ideally with incident data collected over the same period. Any wider rollout should also include a lux audit at the full set of measurement points and a review of the dimming step size. The team's view is that the energy case is strong enough to justify a pilot, but not yet strong enough to justify replacing the fixed schedule across the town.

The report was reviewed by the council's lighting committee in December. The committee asked that the pilot continue in Cinder Row only, and it deferred any decision on Millbank Lane until the second season is complete. Costs, the contractor schedule, and the full logbook are in the appendices.
